originalGroup.material:
A dragon at the classroom door

Our class made a paper dragon for the school festival. It was so long that we could not ____1____ it through the classroom door in one piece. We had not planned the way out.

The festival would begin in an hour. Our teacher asked which parts were joined with ____2____. We found three places where the body could bend without tearing.

Four students held it carefully while another opened both doors. We moved the head through first, then turned the long body. The tail came ____3____. Nobody pulled ahead before the others were ready.

In the hall, we put the dragon back into shape. A younger child asked whether it could dance. We had not planned that, but the body moved nicely when we ____4____ it together. Our teacher checked that we had enough space and that the floor was clear.

Soon we were walking slowly to the drumbeat.  The little child laughed and called her friends to ____5____.

After the festival, we needed somewhere to keep our work. This time, we measured the cupboard ____6____ putting anything inside. We separated the three parts and stored them flat.

I had thought making the dragon was the whole ____7____. Moving it, using it and keeping it safe were part of the job too. At our next project meeting, I asked one more ____8____: "Where will it go when it is finished?" We wrote the answer down. A plan for the ____9____ could be just as useful as a plan for the ____10____.

The train in the shop window

My neighbour Mrs Lane ran a small second-hand shop. She asked me to arrange the window. I found an old toy train in a box and put it on a ____1____ of green paper. I drew hills behind it.

A boy stopped outside. He asked his dad whether the train could move. I reached for it, but Mrs Lane quietly said it had no ____2____. It was a model for display, not a working toy.

I felt bad. My display had made it look ready to run. I wrote a small ____3____ saying, "Display model: does not run." Then I put a book about trains beside it.

The boy came inside. He read the sign and looked at the book. He liked drawing machines. Mrs Lane gave him a spare sheet of paper, and he began to ____4____ the train's wheels.

When he left, he thanked us for letting him look closely. He did not buy the train, but he returned the next week with his ____5____. His wheels were beautifully detailed.

Mrs Lane asked if we could show his picture in the window. With his permission, we put it beside the model.

I had wanted every passer-by to become a ____6____. Now I saw that a shop window could also begin a conversation. We should not, however, ____7____ what an item could do. The sign had helped him enjoy it differently. I kept the hills, but made room for the ____8____. Our train stayed still, yet it had ____9____ someone's imagination. I thought that was a journey worth ____10____.

Posters at the bus shelter

Our art class was asked to design posters for a bus shelter near the school. The council wanted pictures ____1____ would make the waiting area more welcoming. We were told the size of each panel before starting work.

I planned a detailed view of the town. After ____2____ (draw) the first version, I showed it to a classmate. She liked the buildings but asked whether anyone standing several metres away could see the small figures.

We took the page into the corridor and looked at it from a distance. The tiny details almost disappeared. I decided ____3____ (make) the main shapes larger rather than adding more colour to every window.

Our teacher reminded us that a poster was not the same ____4____ a page in a sketchbook. People might see it briefly while getting on a bus. The picture needed to work at that scale and speed.

The final designs ____5____ (print) on suitable material by the council. We did not attach them to the shelter ourselves. A few days later, our class walked past and saw the finished display.

My poster looked ____6____ (bright) than it had in the classroom. More importantly, the main shapes were clear. Two ____7____ (passenger) were looking at another student's picture, and I heard one ask where the place was. That short question made ____8____ (I) smile. The project had taught us to think ____9____ the people who would see our work, not just ourselves. It was ____10____ useful lesson in making a picture for a particular setting.

The wrapper as well as the chocolate

A visitor to our design class brought several empty chocolate wrappers. She asked us ____1____ (compare) them before telling us which products they had contained. Some looked expensive; others seemed intended for a quick snack.

We described the colours and letters ____2____ (careful), then explained what we had assumed about the contents. The visitor reminded us that packaging could create expectations without ____3____ (prove) anything about taste.

Next, we designed a wrapper for a fictional product. Mine used a mountain picture, ____4____ made it look as if the chocolate came from a particular place. I had chosen the picture simply because I liked it. A classmate asked whether a customer might read more into it than I intended.

We discussed the difference ____5____ decoration and a claim. I changed the image and added a clear description of the invented product. The task was not to make the wrapper dull, but to avoid an attractive suggestion that had no basis.

Our final designs ____6____ (display) together at the end of the lesson. We voted for the one with the ____7____ (clear) information of all, not simply the brightest colour. The activity left me more aware of ____8____ (I) own quick judgments. Now, when I buy something, I try to distinguish ____9____ the package actually says from what I imagine. It is ____10____ small habit, but it helps me ask a better question before choosing.
